n:
*On many past occasions *means the time before the Messiah's arrival. For the author of Hebrews, this mainly meant the Old Testament era. During that time, God spoke often and in various ways through:

- dreams,

- visions,

- powerful acts,

- stories,

- commands,

- encouragements,

- angelic appearances, and

- appearances of God himself. 

The prophets were all those people through whom God shared his message (see {{2 Peter 1:19-21|2 Peter 1:19–21}}).
*On many past occasions … but in these last days*: These verses compare two time periods when God spoke. Comparing the two periods side by side shows the differences between them.

Hebrews doesn’t begin like other letters in the New Testament. It doesn’t include greetings to the readers or mention who the writer is.

Instead it talks about who the Son of God is. Jesus shows who God is in the clearest and best way.

All things were created through him. They continue existing because he allows it. Jesus made it possible for people to be freed from the power of sin. This happens when people believe in him.

Then Jesus returned to the Father. The Son of God sits in the place of honour next to God. He has more authority than the angels.

Ancient sermons often began with an introduction. This introduction served two purposes:

- to capture the listener's attention, and 

- to present the main topics.

In Hebrews, the first four verses are a single, elegant Greek sentence. The introduction presents the main idea: God has spoken. Most English translations break these verses into smaller sentences to make them easier to read.

- *These last days* refers to the historical period that began with Christ’s arrival (see {{Isaiah 2:2|Isaiah 2:2}}; {{Acts 2:17|Acts 2:17}}). In the Old Testament era, revelations came in many forms over time. However, God’s ultimate revelation came through his Son, Jesus (see {{Hebrews 2:3-4|Hebrews 2:3–4}}). 

- heir of all things: Christ is God’s royal heir. This is likely a reference to {{Psalm 2:8|Psalm 2:8}}.

- The Greek word translated *radiance* is found only here in the New Testament. It means intense brightness. God's glory shows his presence ({{Exodus 16:7|Exodus 16:7}}; {{Exodus 33:18|33:18}}; {{Isaiah 40:5|Isaiah 40:5}}). The Son's glory reflects God's glory, showing God's presence ({{Luke 9:32|Luke 9:32}}; {{John 1:14|John 1:14}}; {{John 2:11|2:11}}; {{John 17:5|17:5}}; {{Romans 8:17|Romans 8:17}}). 

- The Greek word translated *exact representation* is also unique in the New Testament. It refers to a mark like one on a coin. The Son clearly shows God's character ({{John 1:18|John 1:18}}; {{Philippians 2:6|Philippians 2:6}}; {{Colossians 1:15|Colossians 1:15}}).

- *His powerful word*: This phrase means God's word is a strong and active force that created and controls the world ({{Hebrews 11:3|Hebrews 11:3}}; {{Psalm 33:6-11|Psalm 33:6–11}}). The Son is also called "the Word of God" ({{Revelation 19:13|Revelation 19:13}}; see also {{John 1:1-18|John 1:1–18}}). 

- He cleansed us from our sins (see {{Hebrews 9:11-10:18|Hebrews 9:11–10:18}}). 

- *He sat down*: This refers to {{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}} (see also {{Hebrews 1:13|Hebrews 1:13}}; {{Hebrews 8:1|8:1}}; {{Hebrews 10:12|10:12}}; {{Hebrews 12:2|12:2}}). The Psalm predicted Christ's honor after his suffering (see {{Matthew 22:44|Matthew 22:44}}; {{Acts 2:33|Acts 2:33}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:25|1 Corinthians 15:25}}). The right hand of God shows high honor and position (see {{1 Kings 2:19|1 Kings 2:19}}; {{Psalm 16:11|Psalms 16:11}}; {{Psalm 45:4|45:4}}, {{Psalm 45:9|9}}; {{Psalm 80:17|80:17}}).

- The Son's high position shows that the Son is much greater than the angels in status or rank. First-century Jews admired angels and respected them greatly. By comparing him to the angels, the author of Hebrews emphasizes the Son's superiority over them. 

- *as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs:* Compare {{2 Samuel 7:8-14|2 Samuel 7:8–14}}. Some commentators believe that the title "Son" is the *name* implied here. Others think the name is *Yahweh,* the covenant name of God in the Old Testament ({{Exodus 3:14-15|Exodus 3:14–15}}; compare {{Philippians 2:9-11|Philippians 2:9–11}}).

- *did God ever say*: This verse quotes {{Psalm 2:7|Psalm 2:7}} and {{2 Samuel 7:14|2 Samuel 7:14}}. By raising Jesus to his right hand, the Father declared his special relationship with the Son (see {{Acts 1:9-11|Acts 1:9–11}}; {{Acts 2:32-36|2:32–36}}; {{Acts 7:55-56|7:55–56}}). 

- *Today I have become your Father* (literally *Today I have begotten You*): Jesus did not *become* the Son at the exaltation (when God raised Jesus to heaven and gave him the highest honor). He had been involved in creation ({{Hebrews 1:2|Hebrews 1:2}}). The exaltation confirmed his identity to everyone.

Jesus is greater than God’s angels. The writer of Hebrews used words from the Old Testament to show this in several ways.

Angels are God’s servants. Jesus is God’s Son. Angels worship God. God’s Son is worshipped. Angels serve the King. God’s Son is the King. Angels were created. God’s Son created all things. Everything that God created will be changed. God’s Son remains the same for all time. Angels are messengers who serve people. Jesus is the one who saves people. In every way, Jesus is greater than all that God created.

In these ten verses, the writer uses many Old Testament passages to prove that Jesus is greater than the angels. In ancient Jewish and Christian teaching, people often placed several Old Testament passages together in a row. This practice was called “chain quotations” or “pearl stringing.” The goal was to convince the listeners or readers of a truth by giving a strong group of scriptural proofs at once.

- The supreme (or *firstborn*)* Son* was understood to have certain rights. The firstborn son shared the father's authority. A firstborn also inherited most of the father's property and was especially favored. In the New Testament, "firstborn" often refers to Christ's supreme status in both the church and the world. His resurrection is often cited as proof of this status ({{Acts 13:33|Acts 13:33}}; {{Romans 1:4|Romans 1:4}}; {{Romans 8:29|8:29}}; {{Colossians 1:15|Colossians 1:15}}, {{Colossians 1:18|18}}; {{Revelation 1:5|Revelation 1:5}}; compare {{Hebrews 12:23|Hebrews 12:23}}, where believers are called firstborn children). 

- *"Let all God's angels worship him.": *This quotation from {{Deuteronomy 32:43|Deuteronomy 32:43}} shows that angels are of lower status because they worship the Son (see also {{Psalm 97:7|Psalm 97:7}}).

- This verse quotes {{Psalm 104:4|Psalm 104:4}} to show that angels are messengers or servants. They have a lower rank than the Son, whom they serve. 

- In the Old Testament, angels are sometimes associated with winds and fire (see {{Exodus 3:2|Exodus 3:2}}; {{Judges 6:21|Judges 6:21}}; {{Judges 13:16|13:16}}, {{Judges 13:20|20}}; {{2 Samuel 22:11|2 Samuel 22:11}}; {{Psalm 18:10|Psalms 18:10}}; {{Psalm 35:5|35:5}}). This shows the angels’ connection with God’s rule over nature.

- These verses, quoting {{Psalm 45:6-7|Psalm 45:6–7}}, declare the Son as the divine, just, eternal, anointed King of the universe. 

- *But about the Son He says*: Jesus is called God. In {{Hebrews 1:9|Hebrews 1:9}}, "your God" refers to God the Father. 

- *has anointed you … with the oil of joy*: Olive oil was used to anoint Israel's kings when they began their rule ({{1 Samuel 10:1|1 Samuel 10:1}}; {{1 Kings 19:15-16|1 Kings 19:15–16}}). To anoint someone was to pour oil on that person’s head as a public sign that God had chosen them for a special role. God has anointed his Son, Jesus Christ, as King.

These verses, quoting {{Psalm 102:25-27|Psalm 102:25–27}}, celebrate the Son as both the creator and the one who ends creation. All created things will wear out like old clothing, and the Son will discard them (compare {{Hebrews 2:5|Hebrews 2:5}}; {{2 Peter 3:13|2 Peter 3:13}}; {{Revelation 21:1|Revelation 21:1}}). In contrast, the Son of God will live forever.

- The author ends this series of Old Testament quotes by citing {{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}}. This verse celebrates Christ's exaltation (see also study notes on Luke 20:42–43; 22:69; 1 Corinthians 15:25; Ephesians 1:19–22). 

- The image of the Son's enemies as a footstool under his feet shows their complete defeat (see {{Hebrews 2:8|Hebrews 2:8}}). In ancient times, a victorious king would place his foot on an enemy's neck or back as a sign of control.
*Are not the angels ministering spirits*: The author repeats his conclusion. God sends angels to help his people, who will receive salvation at the end of time (see {{Hebrews 9:28|Hebrews 9:28}}).

- *What we have hear*d is the message of salvation delivered through Christ ({{Hebrews 2:3|Hebrews 2:3}}). 

- *So that we do not drift away* is like a ship going off course. Here, it means losing spiritual focus by not paying close attention to the Good News.

The author argues from a smaller example to a larger one. In the Old Testament era, people who rejected God’s word delivered by angels were punished. If that was true, then the punishment will be even greater for those who now reject the message of salvation. This message has been given by the Son himself and confirmed by the Holy Spirit.

The Law of Moses was given to God’s people. Many Jews believed that God used angels to do this.

When the Israelites didn’t obey the law, they faced the covenant curses. The message of salvation that Jesus brought was greater than the law. So accepting Jesus’ message was even more important than obeying the Mount Sinai covenant.

Jesus had announced the message of the good news of salvation. His disciples and apostles spread the message to others. God showed that Jesus’ message could be trusted. He showed that it was true through Jesus’ miracles.

The Holy Spirit’s work in believers also showed that it was true.

Human beings have less power and authority than angels do. While Jesus lived on earth, he gave up much of his power and authority. That is what it means that Jesus made himself lower than the angels. But after he died God raised him up in victory. That is why the author of Hebrews talked about a crown. Jesus is the King who wears the victory crown. Since his resurrection, he has all of his power and authority again. He will rule completely in the world to come. That is the new creation.

- According to Jewish tradition, God gave the law on Mount Sinai through angelss (see {{Acts 7:38|Acts 7:38}}; {{Galatians 3:19|Galatians 3:19}}). 

- Breaking the law led to punishment (see {{Exodus 22:19|Exodus 22:19}}; {{Leviticus 20:10|Leviticus 20:10}}; {{Numbers 35:16-21|Numbers 35:16–21}}). The punishment could not be escaped (see {{Proverbs 1:24-31|Proverbs 1:24–31}}; {{Jeremiah 11:11|Jeremiah 11:11}}).

- Why do we think we can avoid consequences? The author emphasizes the serious danger of rejecting Christ and his salvation. There is no escape from punishment for those who turn away, and the punishment will be very severe (see {{Hebrews 6:4-12|Hebrews 6:4–12}}; {{Hebrews 10:26-31|10:26–31}}; {{Hebrews 12:29|12:29}}; {{Romans 2:5|Romans 2:5}}; {{1 Thessalonians 2:16|1 Thessalonians 2:16}}). 

- Salvation means God's actions to help his people. For example, God saved his people when he brought them out of Egypt in the exodus ({{Deuteronomy 26:5-9|Deuteronomy 26:5–9}}). In the New Testament, salvation generally refers to Christ's sacrificial death on the cross. This action saved people from the consequences of sin and gave them new life ({{Hebrews 5:9-10|Hebrews 5:9–10}}). Jesus first announced this salvation himself (for example, {{Matthew 4:17|Matthew 4:17}}; {{Matthew 9:35|9:35}}; {{Mark 1:15|Mark 1:15}}; {{Luke 13:1-5|Luke 13:1–5}}). He then confirmed the message through those who heard him speak (for example, {{Mark 6:12|Mark 6:12}}; {{Acts 2:38|Acts 2:38}}; {{Acts 3:19-20|3:19–20}}).

*affirmed by God*: God himself proved the truth of Christ's message and his followers. He provided signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit (see {{Acts 2:22|Acts 2:22}}; {{Romans 15:19|Romans 15:19}}; {{2 Corinthians 12:12|2 Corinthians 12:12}}).

The author of Hebrews uses {{Psalm 8:4-6|Psalm 8:4–6}} to shift from discussing Christ's divine nature in {{Hebrews 1:5-14|Hebrews 1:5}}{{Psalm 8:4-6|–}}{{Hebrews 1:5-14|14}} to his human nature in {{Hebrews 2:10-18|2:10}}{{Psalm 8:4-6|–}}{{Hebrews 2:10-18|18}}. {{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalm 8}} is often paired with {{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}} (see {{Hebrews 1:13|Hebrews 1:13}}) to describe how all creation submits to Christ (see {{1 Corinthians 15:25-27|1 Corinthians 15:25}}{{Psalm 8:4-6|–}}{{1 Corinthians 15:25-27|27}}; {{Ephesians 1:20-23|Ephesians 1:20}}{{Psalm 8:4-6|–}}{{Ephesians 1:20-23|23}}). Christ is the perfect human. In his exaltation, he achieves true dominion over creation, something humanity could not do.

- *What is man*: These lines of the psalm highlight God's special care for humans. 

- *the son of Man*: The term *son of man* refers to human life and is similar to *man* in the previous line. In the Gospels, Jesus often used this phrase to describe himself.

These verses quote {{Psalm 8:4-6|Psalm 8:4–6}}. {{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalm 8}} talks about the position God has given to humanity. The author of Hebrews uses the verse to predict Christ, who fulfills and represents humanity.

- *him:* This refers to all of humanity and specifically to Christ (see study note on 2:6–8). 

- Christ became *a little lower than the angels *(or *a little while lower*). In other words, Christ became like other humans (see also {{Philippians 2:5-8|Philippians 2:5–8}}). 

- *crowned him with glory and honor*: Because of his suffering, he was given the highest honor and praise (see {{Hebrews 2:9|Hebrews 2:9}}; {{Philippians 2:9-11|Philippians 2:9–11}}).

- *placed everything under his feet*: See study note on 2:6–8. 

- *He left nothing outside of his control*: All things are ultimately under the authority of Christ and the church. However, we have not yet seen this fully happen. Only at the end of the age (the final period of time when Jesus returns) will it be completed.

*But we see Jesus*: How can the church continue when evil and death exist? We look to Jesus in his human life, where he was "a little lower than the angels." We also look to him in his exaltation, where he is now "crowned with glory and honor." His suffering as a human led to his exaltation (see {{Philippians 2:5-11|Philippians 2:5–11}}; compare {{Isaiah 52:13-53:12|Isaiah 52:13–53:12}}). See also {{Hebrews 12:1-13|Hebrews 12:1–13}}.

- *sons*: The author uses the title *Son* for Jesus and refers to God's people as *sons*. The translation *children* clarifies that it includes all of God's people, both male and female. 

- The term *author* had many meanings in the ancient world. It could also mean *founder, hero, champion, prince, captain, leader,* or *scout.* Jesus is called the *author* because he began the work of salvation and guides people to glory.

As God’s Son, Jesus is the older brother of all of God’s children. Jesus is the first human being who wasn’t a slave to the fear of death. He knew he would rise from the dead with eternal life. He wasn’t a slave to the devil’s power. He lived free from the power of sin.

These things are all part of what salvation means. Since Jesus has gone through them first, he can lead others through them. Jesus lived a fully human life on earth. There is nothing that human beings go through that he can’t understand. What he suffered as a human being made him perfect or complete. It made him able to help human beings exactly the way they need to be helped.

As a human being, Jesus did the job of the high priest. He offered the sacrifice to pay for people’s sins. The sacrifice that he offered was himself. His death made salvation possible for all who believe in him.

This passage suggests at least four reasons why the Son of God became human. 

- It was appropriate: It aligns with God's character to achieve salvation this way ({{Hebrews 2:10|Hebrews 2:10}}). 

- Jesus needed to become human to die ({{Hebrews 2:14|2:14}}). 

- According to Old Testament law, high priests had to be chosen from among God's people ({{Hebrews 2:17|2:17}}). 

- Jesus became a compassionate priest by experiencing human suffering and challenges ({{Hebrews 2:18|2:18}}).

- *of the same family* (literally *are all out of one*): In this context, "Father" likely refers to God. However, the author might have been thinking of Abraham as a shared ancestor (see {{Hebrews 2:16|Hebrews 2:16}}) or of human nature as a shared experience (*out of one nature*). 

- *brothers*: The Greek word *adelphoi *is a general term for family members, both male and female.

This verse quotes {{Psalm 22:22|Psalm 22:22}} and discusses the term brothers and sisters in {{Hebrews 2:11|Hebrews 2:11}}. {{Psalm 22:1-31|Psalm 22}} includes important prophecies about Christ's suffering ({{Psalm 22:1|Psalm 22:1}}, {{Psalm 22:7-8|7–8}}, {{Psalm 22:16-18|16}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Psalm 22:16-18|18}}; see {{Matthew 27:35|Matthew 27:35}}, {{Matthew 27:43|43}}; {{John 19:23-24|John 19:23}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{John 19:23-24|24}}, {{John 19:31-36|31}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{John 19:31-36|36}}). {{Psalm 22:22|Psalm 22:22}} highlights how the righteous sufferer (Jesus) joins God's people in praising God for His help.

- This verse quotes {{Isaiah 8:17-18|Isaiah 8:17}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Isaiah 8:17-18|18}}, which is part of a larger context about the Messiah (compare {{Isaiah 8:14|Isaiah 8:14}} with {{Romans 9:33|Romans 9:33}}; {{1 Peter 2:8|1 Peter 2:8}}). 

- *"I will put my trust in Him."*: This shows that Jesus trusts God the Father. 

- *"I, and the children God has given Me."*: This shows the close relationship between Jesus and God's children.

- The death of the Son of God as a sacrifice for sin weakened the devil's power. It made the devil's power over death ineffective ({{1 Corinthians 15:56|1 Corinthians 15:56}}). 

- Philo, a first-century Jewish philosopher, wrote that "nothing enslaves the mind like fearing death" (Philo, *That Every Good Person Is Free* 3.22). Through his sacrificial death, Christ freed those who were slaves to the fear of dying.
*descendants of Abraham:* Jesus died on the cross for those who inherit God's promises to Abraham, not for the angels.

- These verses introduce Jesus as our kind and loyal high priest, a role fully explained in the main part of Hebrews ({{Hebrews 4:14-10:25|Hebrews 4:14–10:25}}). 

- He needed to share our human experience (see {{Hebrews 5:1|5:1}}).

- *holy brothers*: In ancient times, speakers and writers often called religious groups "brothers" (Greek *adelphoi*), including both men and women. Many modern translations use "brothers and sisters."

- *set your focus on Jesus*: Focusing on Jesus helps you stay strong in your faith ({{Hebrews 2:9|Hebrews 2:9}}; {{Hebrews 12:1-2|12:1–2}}). 

- *the apostle*: This term may emphasize the Son’s role in sharing God’s name and message ({{Hebrews 2:12|2:12}}; {{Matthew 10:40|Matt 10:40}}; {{Mark 9:37|Mark 9:37}}; {{Luke 10:16|Luke 10:16}}).

The author compares Jesus to Moses, presenting Jesus as the ultimate example of faithfulness. Moses was a highly honored leader in Judaism. His respected status is used to show that Jesus is even greater than Moses.

The author of Hebrews described Moses as a faithful servant in God’s house. God’s house was a way to talk about God’s family. It was also a way to describe the holy tent and the temple.

In God’s house, Jesus is more than a servant. He is the Son. Through Jesus, God’s house is more than the holy tent or the temple. It’s made up of all who follow Jesus faithfully and with hope.

The story of Israel is a warning and an example for the followers of Jesus. Over and over again the Israelites refused to listen to Moses. Again and again they refused to obey God’s word. As a result many of them didn’t enter the land that God had promised them.

Some of those who heard the message of Hebrews were Jewish believers. They honoured Moses and the Law of Moses. But the writer of Hebrews urged them to be even more committed to Jesus. He called Jesus their apostle and high priest. They must hold onto their hope and faith in Christ.

Jesus was loyal to God and the mission given to him by the Father ({{Hebrews 5:7-10|Hebrews 5:7}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Hebrews 5:7-10|10}}; {{Hebrews 12:1-3|12:1}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Hebrews 12:1-3|3}}; {{Philippians 2:5-11|Philippians 2:5}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Philippians 2:5-11|11}}), just like Moses was ({{Numbers 12:7|Numbers 12:7}}). Many Jews in the first century saw Moses as the greatest person in history, even more important than angels.

Jesus deserves more glory for two reasons:

- A person who builds a house deserves more praise than the house itself. The Messiah is the one who builds God’s house (see {{2 Samuel 7:13|2 Samuel 7:13}}). This implies that Moses is part of the house (God’s people) that God has built. 

- While Moses was a servant in God’s house, Christ, as the Son, is the heir in charge of God’s entire house. Sons have a higher status than household servants.

We belong to God's house if we act courageously. The author could not fully assure those who were drifting away from Christ and the church. Those who continue in faith can be sure they are part of God's house (see {{Hebrews 3:14|Hebrews 3:14}}; {{Romans 8:9|Romans 8:9}}, {{Romans 8:17|17}}; {{Romans 11:22|11:22}}; {{2 Corinthians 13:5|2 Corinthians 13:5}}; {{Colossians 1:22-23|Colossians 1:22}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Colossians 1:22-23|23}}).

This passage serves as a warning, showing the negative example of those who wandered in the wilderness for forty years and died there. The wilderness wanderings symbolize disobedience to God and its consequences (see {{Numbers 32:7-11|Numbers 32:7}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Numbers 32:7-11|11}}; {{Deuteronomy 1:19-35|Deuteronomy 1:19}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Deuteronomy 1:19-35|35}}; {{Psalm 106:24-26|Psalm 106:24}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Psalm 106:24-26|26}}).

The Israelites rebelled and tested God in places like Massah and Meribah, where water was scarce ({{Exodus 17:1-7|Exodus 17:1}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Exodus 17:1-7|7}}; {{Numbers 20:2-13|Numbers 20:2}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Numbers 20:2-13|13}}). They especially disobeyed at Kadesh by refusing to enter the promised land ({{Hebrews 3:10|Hebrews 3:10}}; see {{Numbers 14:1-25|Numbers 14:1}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Numbers 14:1-25|25}}; {{Deuteronomy 1:19-46|Deuteronomy 1:19}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Deuteronomy 1:19-46|46}}; {{Psalm 106:1-48|Psalm 106}}).

Even after witnessing the miracles God performed for them, the people of Israel tested God's patience by not trusting him in the wilderness ({{Numbers 14:11|Numbers 14:11}}, {{Numbers 14:22|22}}). Their rebellion stemmed from their hearts consistently turning away from God. They did not want to obey God. As a result, God became angry with them.

- Rebellion has consequences.

- God’s anger is not just an emotional reaction. It is his fair and just response to sin ({{John 3:36|John 3:36}}; {{Romans 1:18|Romans 1:18}}; {{1 Thessalonians 2:16|1 Thessalonians 2:16}}). 

- God's promise (see {{Hebrews 6:13-20|Hebrews 6:13}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Hebrews 6:13-20|20}}; {{Hebrews 7:20-22|7:20}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|22}}, {{Hebrews 7:28|28}}) was that they would never enter Canaan, the land of rest from their travels ({{Deuteronomy 1:19-46|Deuteronomy 1:19}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Deuteronomy 1:19-46|46}}; {{Deuteronomy 3:20|3:20}}; {{Deuteronomy 12:10|12:10}}; {{Joshua 1:13|Joshua 1:13}}).
*heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God*: An evil heart stubbornly resists the Lord because of unbelief, leading a person to turn away from the living God.

The author of Hebrews points to important words from {{Psalm 95:1-11|Psalm 95}}. These include *heart, today, hear, enter, rest*, and *unbelief*. In the ancient world, Bible teachers would cite a passage from the Old Testament and then explain it. They often highlighted key words from the passage, much like preachers do today. This style of explanation was called *midrash* (a type of Jewish Bible interpretation).
The author uses the word "today" from {{Psalm 95:7|Psalms 95:7}} to urge people to remind each other daily about the misleading and toughening effects of sin.

If we stay faithful, we can be sure we belong to God's family (see {{Hebrews 3:6|Hebrews 3:6}}; {{Romans 8:9|Romans 8:9}}, {{Romans 8:17|17}}; {{Romans 11:22|11:22}}; {{2 Corinthians 13:5|2 Corinthians 13:5}}; {{Colossians 1:22-23|Colossians 1:22}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Colossians 1:22-23|23}}).
This verse quotes {{Psalm 95:7-8|Psalm 95:7–8}}, urging readers to listen and respond positively to God's voice. It summarizes the author's message in {{Hebrews 3:12-14|Hebrews 3:12–14}}.

These verses use a series of quick questions and answers, a common rhetorical method. The three questions follow the ideas in {{Psalm 95:8-11|Psalm 95:8}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Psalm 95:8-11|11}}: The people of Israel rebelled against God, God was angry, and God swore they would never enter his rest. The answers come from other Old Testament passages about the Israelites' rebellion in the wilderness ({{Numbers 14:1-45|Numbers 14}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:1-29|Deuteronomy 9}}; {{Psalm 106:1-48|Psalm 106}}). The author emphasizes the severe consequences of disobeying God.

In Hebrews and the Old Testament, unbelief and disobedience are closely linked ({{Numbers 14:11|Numbers 14:11}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:23|Deuteronomy 9:23}}; {{Psalm 78:22|Psalm 78:22}}, {{Psalm 78:32|32}}). Because of their disobedience, they could not enter God's rest by entering the land of Canaan ({{Deuteronomy 3:20|Deuteronomy 3:20}}; {{Deuteronomy 12:10|12:10}}; {{Joshua 1:13|Joshua 1:13}}).
*let us be careful*: Fearing God means having a deep respect and awe for God and God's will. Missing out on God's promises would be a great tragedy.
The author moves to the promise that the faithful will enter God's rest and urges listeners to take this promise seriously. Hearing alone is not enough. Listening must be combined with faith.

Long ago God invited his people Israel to enter his rest. This good news was spoken in the time of Moses.

Joshua led the people of Israel into the land of Canaan. During this time they had rest from slavery. But true and lasting rest comes only from believing in Jesus and following him. This is the rest that God invites everyone to enjoy.

God sees and knows everything about all that he created. He uses his words and the message about Jesus to show what is in people’s hearts. That’s how the word of God is like a sword that is alive and active.

This was a way to warn and encourage the believers hearing the message of Hebrews. The author wanted them to make every effort to obey Jesus.

- This good news is the message of salvation ({{Hebrews 2:3-4|Hebrews 2:3}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Hebrews 2:3-4|4}}).

- They lacked the faith of those who listened to God. Some manuscripts say *they didn’t combine what they heard with faith.* In both cases, the listeners had weak faith and did not trust God's promise.

- People who believe the good news are the true heirs of God's rest, which is the salvation offered through Christ's sacrifice. 

- *God has said*: The quote from {{Psalm 95:11|Psalm 95:11}} reminds us that the unbelieving rebels in the wilderness would never enter God's place of rest (compare {{Hebrews 11:8|Hebrews 11:8}}, {{Hebrews 11:10|10}}, {{Hebrews 11:14-16|14}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Hebrews 11:14-16|16}}; {{Hebrews 12:22-24|12:22}}{{Psalm 22:7-8|–}}{{Hebrews 12:22-24|24}}). 

- *since the foundation of the world*: God's rest means much more than just entering Canaan (see study note on 4:4).
This verse quotes {{Genesis 2:2|Genesis 2:2}} to show that God created rest when he rested after creation.
This quote from {{Psalm 95:11|Psalm 95:11}} repeats the idea found in {{Hebrews 4:3|Hebrews 4:3}}.

*it remains for some to enter His rest*: Building on the discussion in {{Hebrews 4:3-5|Hebrews 4:3–5}}, the author will argue that the promised rest is still open ({{Hebrews 4:7-10|4:7}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 4:7-10|10}}). Those who wandered in the wilderness heard the good news that the promised land was open to them. They were not able to enter because they disobeyed God (see {{Numbers 14:1-25|Numbers 14:1}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Numbers 14:1-25|25}}; {{Deuteronomy 1:19-46|Deuteronomy 1:19}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Deuteronomy 1:19-46|46}}; {{Psalm 106:1-48|Psalm 106}}).

*God again designated a certain day as “Today,”*: David wrote {{Psalm 95:1-11|Psalm 95}} long after the events in the wilderness, so God's rest is not just for that earlier generation. The words from {{Psalm 95:7-8|Psalm 95:7}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Psalm 95:7-8|8}} urge us not to harden our hearts when we hear God's voice, so we can enter the rest that the people in the wilderness missed. This chance is available today (see {{Hebrews 3:13|Hebrews 3:13}}).

Joshua and Jesus share the same name (Greek *Iēsous,* Hebrew *Yehoshua‘*). In the Old Testament, it is usually translated as *Joshua*, and in the New Testament, as *Jesus* (see also study note on Exodus 17:9). The author is making a wordplay on their shared name. Joshua led God's people into the promised land ({{Joshua 3:1-4:24|Joshua 3–4}}), but God meant more when he promised rest. Jesus provides God's ultimate rest ({{Hebrews 3:13-14|Hebrews 3:13}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 3:13-14|14}}; {{Hebrews 4:3|4:3}}, {{Hebrews 4:9-11|9}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 4:9-11|11}}, {{Hebrews 4:14-16|14}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 4:14-16|16}}).

*a Sabbath rest*: The sacrifice of Jesus worked like a Day of Atonement sacrifice ({{Hebrews 5:1-3|Hebrews 5:1}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 5:1-3|3}}; {{Hebrews 9:13-22|9:13}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 9:13-22|22}}; see {{Leviticus 23:26-28|Leviticus 23:26}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Leviticus 23:26-28|28}}, {{Leviticus 23:32|32}}). Through Christ's sacrifice, God's promised rest is available to his people.

- *rests from his own work*: See {{Exodus 20:8-11|Exodus 20:8}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Exodus 20:8-11|11}}. 

- *just as God did*: {{Genesis 2:2|Genesis 2:2}}.

- *make every effort to enter*: If we do not actively obey God's voice and respond to the good news ({{Hebrews 4:1-2|Hebrews 4:1}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 4:1-2|2}}), we will face consequences like the wilderness wanderers did. We will fall. 

- *us … no one*: Obedience is not just a personal issue. God's people have a shared responsibility to obey and should support each other in this effort (compare {{Hebrews 3:13|3:13}}; {{Hebrews 10:25|10:25}}; {{Hebrews 12:15|12:15}}).

The author urges us to listen to God's voice, as mentioned in {{Hebrews 3:7|Hebrews 3:7}}, {{Hebrews 3:15|15}}, and {{Hebrews 4:7|4:7}}, quoting {{Psalm 95:7|Psalm 95:7}}. They describe God's word as alive and powerful, meaning it is an active and effective force. The word that created and controls the universe ({{Hebrews 1:2-3|Hebrews 1:2}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 1:2-3|3}}) can also strongly influence people. It is like the sharpest two-edged sword, able to reach the deepest parts of people's lives and reveal their thoughts and desires (see {{Ephesians 6:17|Ephesians 6:17}}; {{Revelation 1:16|Revelation 1:16}}; {{Revelation 2:12|2:12}}, {{Revelation 2:16|16}}; {{Revelation 19:15|19:15}}).
*Uncovered and exposed* means feeling vulnerable, helpless, or unprotected. The guilty cannot hide from God's powerful judgment (see {{Revelation 3:17|Revelation 3:17}}).

- This verse sums up the message and challenge of Hebrews. Jesus, the Son of God, is our high priest and the reason to stay strong in the Christian faith. 

- *a great high priest*: Israel’s high priest was the main leader in worship and the mediator between God and the people (see {{Exodus 31:10|Exodus 31:10}}; {{Leviticus 4:3|Leviticus 4:3}}; {{2 Kings 12:10|2 Kings 12:10}}; {{2 Chronicles 26:20|2 Chronicles 26:20}}). 

- *who has passed through the heavens*: Earthly high priests entered God’s presence in the Most Holy Place once a year on the Day of Atonement ({{Leviticus 16:1-25|Leviticus 16:1}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Leviticus 16:1-25|25}}). In contrast, Jesus, our high priest, has entered God’s presence in heaven and stays there ({{Hebrews 7:26|Hebrews 7:26}}; {{Hebrews 9:11-12|9:11}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 9:11-12|12}}, {{Hebrews 9:23-26|23}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 9:23-26|26}}).

- *let us hold firmly*: Stay committed to actively believing in and being loyal to Jesus (see also {{Colossians 2:19|Colossians 2:19}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:15|2 Thessalonians 2:15}}; {{Revelation 2:13|Revelation 2:13}}, {{Revelation 2:25|25}}; {{Revelation 3:11|3:11}}).

These important verses finish the encouragement that began at {{Hebrews 3:1|Hebrews 3:1}}. They also introduce a long teaching about Jesus and his role as high priest ({{Hebrews 4:14-10:25|4:14–10:25}}).

God appointed Jesus to be the high priest. When he lived on earth, Jesus went through things that all people go through. He was born as a baby and learnt things as he grew up. At times he was weak and hurting. At times he was tempted and tested but he never sinned. At times he suffered.

All throughout his life he learnt how to obey God while being a human being. His understanding of what life is like for human beings is complete. This is what it means that he was made perfect. As their priest, Jesus deals gently with believers. This gives believers the boldness to come to God. Believers can trust that God will show them grace and mercy.

- Our high priest understands our weaknesses and our tendency to sin because he faced the same challenges. He was tempted by lust, greed, unforgiveness, and dishonesty. This makes him compassionate as our high priest ({{Hebrews 5:2|Hebrews 5:2}}). 

- *yet was without sin*: Jesus is different from earthly high priests, who had to make offerings for their own sins before they could make offerings for the people ({{Hebrews 5:3|5:3}}; {{Hebrews 7:26-28|7:26}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 7:26-28|28}}; see also {{1 Peter 2:22-23|1 Peter 2:22}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{1 Peter 2:22-23|23}}).

- The verb translated as *let us then approach* can also mean "let us continually come," indicating ongoing action. 

- As our compassionate high priest, Jesus has made it possible for people to confidently enter God's presence (see {{Hebrews 6:19-20|Hebrews 6:19}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 6:19-20|20}}; {{Hebrews 10:19-23|10:19}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 10:19-23|23}}). There, we can receive his mercy and grace when we need it most.

- *Every high priest*: This phrase outlines what high priests must do. 

- *among men*: The high priest was one of the people, so Jesus needed to become human (see {{Hebrews 2:17-18|Hebrews 2:17}}{{Hebrews 4:3-5|–}}{{Hebrews 2:17-18|18}}). 

- Another requirement for high priests was to represent others by offering sacrifices for them ({{Hebrews 7:25-28|7:25–28}}). Only the high priest could offer the sacrifice on the Day of Atonement ({{Exodus 29:1-46|Exodus 29}}; {{Leviticus 16:1-25|Leviticus 16:1–25}}).
This section discusses how the Son of God became a superior high priest. The main text is {{Psalm 110:4|Psalm 110:4}}, where God promises that the Son will be a priest forever like Melchizedek.
A high priest could be kind to those who sin because he also had weaknesses, meaning he was sinful ({{Hebrews 5:3|Hebrews 5:3}}; compare {{Hebrews 4:15|4:15}}).
On the Day of Atonement, the high priest had to offer sacrifices for himself and his family before offering sacrifices for the people ({{Leviticus 16:11|Leviticus 16:11}}).
God appoints the high priest, not humans (see {{Exodus 28:1|Exodus 28:1}}; {{Leviticus 8:1-12|Leviticus 8:1–12}}; {{Numbers 16:1-26|Numbers 16:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Numbers 16:1-26|26}}).

The author connects {{Psalm 2:7|Psalms 2:7}} and {{Psalm 110:4|110:4}} because both passages feature God speaking to his Son. The exalted Son, who became human ({{Hebrews 1:1-2:18|Hebrews 1–2}}), is appointed by God to a special high priesthood.

The phrase *with loud cries and tears* likely refers to the suffering Jesus experienced in the garden of Gethsemane (see {{Matthew 26:36-46|Matthew 26:36}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Matthew 26:36-46|46}}; {{Mark 14:32-42|Mark 14:32}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Mark 14:32-42|42}}; {{Luke 22:40-46|Luke 22:40}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Luke 22:40-46|46}}). God heard his prayers by affirming his righteousness and his role as high priest. Jesus showed faithful devotion to God. His example encourages the readers to remain faithful as well (compare {{Hebrews 12:2-3|Hebrews 12:2}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 12:2-3|3}}).

The suffering of Jesus was the basis for his higher role as a priest. His humiliation and suffering came before his rise to glory ({{Hebrews 2:9|Hebrews 2:9}}; {{Philippians 2:5-11|Philippians 2:5}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Philippians 2:5-11|11}}).

He learned obedience through his suffering. Jesus was always obedient, even before his suffering. He lived his human life, including his death on the cross, fully submitting to God's will. We are expected to follow the same path ({{Hebrews 12:1-11|Hebrews 12:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 12:1-11|11}}).

- *And having been made perfect*: In Hebrews, *perfect* means "complete" or "mature" (see {{Hebrews 2:10|Hebrews 2:10}}; {{Hebrews 5:14|5:14}}; {{Hebrews 7:11|7:11}}; {{Hebrews 9:9-11|9:9}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 9:9-11|11}}). Jesus became the source of eternal salvation for everyone who obeys him through his sufferings. 

- As the Son obeyed the Father ({{Hebrews 5:8|5:8}}), fully following the Father's will, those seeking *salvation* must *obey him.*
*high priest in the order of Melchizedek*: See {{Hebrews 7:1-28|Hebrews 7:1–28}} for more details.
*dull of hearing*: The Greek term means "slow, not very smart, careless, or lazy."
This message addresses the spiritual laziness of the recipients.

The author of Hebrews described what growing up in faith means. When someone starts following Jesus, they are like a spiritual baby. They learn the basic teachings about Jesus. And they keep growing spiritually.

They are to continue learning with faith and patience for the rest of their lives. If they stop wanting to understand what Jesus wants to teach them, they stop growing. The author also spoke about falling away from the faith. This happens when believers no longer want God’s light in their lives.

They no longer look forward to the age to come with hope. The age to come was another way of talking about the new creation. They no longer want the Holy Spirit to be working in them. This leads to living in ways that are sinful and aren’t godly. The author described those ways like a field that produces thorns and weeds.

The author wanted the believers to be like a field that produces a good crop. Some of them were already doing this in the ways they showed that they loved God.

After starting to talk about the role of Jesus as high priest ({{Hebrews 5:1-10|Hebrews 5:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 5:1-10|10}}), the author addresses the audience with several encouragements ({{Hebrews 5:11-6:20|5:11–6:20}}). This change in the sermon or speech aimed to capture the listeners' attention.

- Their lack of spiritual energy was surprising because they had been believers for so long. They should have been spiritual leaders teaching others from their knowledge and Christian experience. 

- *the basic principles*: The simplest parts of the Christian faith (see {{Hebrews 6:1-3|Hebrews 6:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 6:1-3|3}}). 

- The imagery of milk and solid food was used to separate basic from advanced education, and immature from mature students.
Knowing the difference between right and wrong shows spiritual maturity.

- *go on*: Or *let us be carried on,* suggesting that God starts our growth to maturity ({{Philippians 2:12-13|Philippians 2:12}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Philippians 2:12-13|13}}) and that it is a continuous journey. 

- Repentance and faith are the fundamental commitments that introduce a person to the new covenant and form the basic stance of a Christian’s life (see {{Acts 20:21|Acts 20:21}}).

Because the hearers' are not mature ({{Hebrews 5:11-14|Hebrews 5:11}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 5:11-14|14}}), the author encourages them to go beyond basic teachings. These six basic teachings were fundamental parts of Jewish instruction. The author may be urging them to deepen their understanding of Christ, which he explains further in {{Hebrews 7:1-10:25|7:1–10:25}}.

- The term *baptisms* (or washings) is plural, indicating it means more than just Christian baptism. In first-century Judaism, teachings about different washings were common (see {{Matthew 15:2|Matthew 15:2}}; {{Mark 7:3|Mark 7:3}}). The author might also refer to the cleansing rituals from the Old Testament (compare {{Hebrews 9:13|Hebrews 9:13}}; {{Hebrews 10:22|10:22}}). 

- The laying on of hands was linked to:

- healing ({{Mark 5:22-23|Mark 5:22}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Mark 5:22-23|23}}; {{Luke 13:13|Luke 13:13}}), 

- ritual blessing ({{Matthew 19:13|Matthew 19:13}}, {{Matthew 19:15|15}}), r

- eceiving the Holy Spirit ({{Acts 8:17|Acts 8:17}}; {{Acts 9:17|9:17}}; {{Acts 19:6|19:6}}), and 

- recognizing a person’s ministry ({{Acts 6:6|Acts 6:6}}; {{Acts 13:3|13:3}}). 

- Resurrection of the dead: See “The Resurrection of the Dead” Theme Note. 

- *eternal judgment*: See {{Revelation 20:11-15|Revelation 20:11}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Revelation 20:11-15|15}}.

The author is encouraging readers to grow up, not just in understanding but in all aspects (see {{Hebrews 4:11|Hebrews 4:11}}; {{Hebrews 5:14|5:14}}; {{Hebrews 10:23-39|10:23}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 10:23-39|39}}; {{Hebrews 12:1-13|12:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 12:1-13|13}}).

- In Greek, the word translated *impossible* starts the sentence for emphasis. It means this absolutely cannot happen (see also {{Hebrews 6:18|Hebrews 6:18}}; {{Hebrews 10:4|10:4}}; {{Hebrews 11:6|11:6}}). 

- They were once enlightened when they "first learned about Christ" (see {{Hebrews 10:32|10:32}} and corresponding study note). 

- The good things of heaven might refer to the manna given from heaven ({{Exodus 16:4|Exodus 16:4}}, {{Exodus 16:15|15}}; {{Psalm 78:24|Psalm 78:24}}) as a symbol of spiritual blessings.

This passage is one of the most challenging in the New Testament. It warns about those who have abandoned the Christian faith. Those who have turned away from Christ and the church are like those who fell in the wilderness ({{Hebrews 3:15-19|Hebrews 3:15}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 3:15-19|19}}). Their lack of faith leads to severe judgment (compare {{Hebrews 10:26-31|10:26}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 10:26-31|31}}).

- *who have tasted the goodness of the word of God*: These people heard God's word preached ({{Hebrews 2:3-4|Hebrews 2:3}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 2:3-4|4}}; {{Hebrews 4:1-2|4:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 4:1-2|2}}) and saw its impact. 

- *the powers of the coming age*: They witnessed signs and wonders when they heard the good news ({{Hebrews 2:4|2:4}}; compare {{Exodus 7:3-4|Exodus 7:3}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Exodus 7:3-4|4}}; {{Deuteronomy 7:19|Deuteronomy 7:19}}; {{Psalm 66:3|Psalms 66:3}}; {{Psalm 77:15-20|77:15}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Psalm 77:15-20|20}}; {{Psalm 78:9-16|78:9}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Psalm 78:9-16|16}}; {{1 Corinthians 10:1-13|1 Corinthians 10:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{1 Corinthians 10:1-13|13}}).

- *then have fallen away*: This image reminds us of the people in the wilderness who disobeyed God and perished in the desert ({{Hebrews 3:17|Hebrews 3:17}}; {{Hebrews 4:11|4:11}}; {{Numbers 14:1-4|Numbers 14:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Numbers 14:1-4|4}}, {{Numbers 14:29-30|29}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Numbers 14:29-30|30}}). 

- *to be restored to repentance*: They had repented before but showed no results from it ({{Hebrews 6:7-8|Hebrews 6:7}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 6:7-8|8}}). When people reject Christ and his ultimate sacrifice, they cannot find another way to repent. 

- Rejecting the Son of God is like nailing him to the cross again. Crucifixion was the worst form of rejection and shame in the Greco-Roman world. Those who turned away from Christ were like those who mocked him at the cross, denying he was the Messiah and Son of God, and instead deserving of shame (see {{Matthew 27:39-44|Matthew 27:39}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Matthew 27:39-44|44}}).

*land*: Fertile land symbolizes blessing, while barren land with thorns and thistles represents a curse. Burning such a field symbolizes judgment ({{2 Samuel 23:4-7|2 Samuel 23:4}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{2 Samuel 23:4-7|7}}; {{Isaiah 10:17|Isaiah 10:17}}; {{Isaiah 33:12|33:12}}; {{Ezekiel 19:12-13|Ezekiel 19:12}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Ezekiel 19:12-13|13}}; {{Matthew 3:10|Matthew 3:10}}).

- *we are convinced*: Skilled speakers and writers show confidence in their audience to inspire them (see {{Romans 15:14|Romans 15:14}}). 

- The author believes his hearers' lives show they truly know God, including their salvation. In the New Testament, salvation mainly refers to Christ’s work on the cross ({{Hebrews 5:9-10|Hebrews 5:9}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 5:9-10|10}}; see also study note on 2:3). Hebrews highlights the completion of salvation at the end of time ({{Hebrews 9:28|9:28}}).

After giving a strong warning to his hearers ({{Hebrews 6:4-8|Hebrews 6:4}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 6:4-8|8}}), the author now softens it by calling them *beloved*. He shows confidence in them and offers more encouragement.

*He will not forget your work*: By showing love for God and his people, your actions prove your true connection with God ({{Romans 2:6-7|Romans 2:6}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Romans 2:6-7|7}}; {{1 Corinthians 3:13-15|1 Corinthians 3:13}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{1 Corinthians 3:13-15|15}}; {{James 2:14-20|James 2:14}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{James 2:14-20|20}}). God remembers ({{Exodus 2:24|Exodus 2:24}}; {{1 Chronicles 16:15|1 Chronicles 16:15}}; {{Psalm 106:45|Psalm 106:45}}) and recognizes those who truly belong to him.

*show this same diligence* (literally *show the same eager commitment*): Loving other believers is a key sign of true Christian faith ({{James 2:15-16|James 2:15}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{James 2:15-16|16}}; {{1 John 3:16-20|1 John 3:16}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{1 John 3:16-20|20}}). By being diligent and committed, they can be sure of their hope in Christ. Perseverance brings assurance of salvation.

A strong commitment ({{Hebrews 6:10-11|Hebrews 6:10}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 6:10-11|11}}) helps prevent spiritual dullness ({{Hebrews 5:11-12|5:11}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 5:11-12|12}}). By loving God and others, we follow the example of great faith leaders. The author stresses that faith and endurance are essential for God's people (see {{Hebrews 11:4-38|11:4}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 11:4-38|38}}).

Abraham was a leading example of faith. He believed God would give him a son and was ready to sacrifice that son to obey God ({{Hebrews 11:17-19|Hebrews 11:17}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 11:17-19|19}}; {{Genesis 15:1-5|Genesis 15:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Genesis 15:1-5|5}}; {{Genesis 22:1-14|22:1}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Genesis 22:1-14|14}}). Because of Abraham's faith, God promised to bless him and increase his descendants.

God had made a promise to Abraham in his covenant with Abraham.

The believers reading the letter of Hebrews knew this. They also knew that God had kept his promise to Abraham. He had blessed Abraham with a very large family that became the nation of Israel.

The author of Hebrews used this story to remind the readers about God’s promises. God never lies. He always keeps his promises. His purpose for the world doesn’t change. His purpose is for his creation to live in peace with him for ever.

This is the hope that believers have. This hope is certain and secure because it’s based on Jesus’ work.

This passage highlights how we can trust God's promises. It uses an example ({{Hebrews 6:13-15|Hebrews 6:13}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 6:13-15|15}}), then explains a general rule ({{Hebrews 6:16|6:16}}), and finally makes the main point: God made an important promise ({{Hebrews 6:17-18|6:17}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 6:17-18|18}}). This promise gives us hope because it shows Jesus is our eternal high priest ({{Hebrews 6:19-20|6:19}}{{Leviticus 8:1-12|–}}{{Hebrews 6:19-20|20}}).
God promised to make Abraham a great nation through Isaac ({{Exodus 1:7|Exodus 1:7}}).

- In human relationships, when people take an oath, it is considered binding. If oaths assure truth among humans, an oath from God should inspire even more confidence ({{Hebrews 6:17-19|Hebrews 6:17–19}}).

- *someone greater than themselves*: Compare with {{Hebrews 6:13|6:13}}.

- God also made a promise with an oath (a solemn promise), see {{Hebrews 7:20-22|Hebrews 7:20–22}}. This oath shows that God will never change his mind because it is impossible for God to lie (see {{Psalm 110:4|Psalm 110:4}}). 

- *We who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us*, similiar to people in the Old Testament who accidentally killed someone and sought refuge ({{Numbers 35:9-34|Numbers 35:9}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Numbers 35:9-34|34}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:41-43|Deuteronomy 4:41}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Deuteronomy 4:41-43|43}}). Christ is like a city of refuge, where believers find safety from God's anger. Because of this, Christ's followers have great confidence.

- Christian hope is a reliable anchor for our souls. In the first century, an anchor symbolized stability and safety. 

- *behind the curtain*: A curtain separated the outer room of the sanctuary, where only priests could enter, from the inner room, the Most Holy Place ({{Exodus 25:10-40|Exodus 25:10}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 25:10-40|40}}). Only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, and only once a year on the Day of Atonement ({{Exodus 29:1-46|Exodus 29}}; {{Leviticus 16:1-25|Leviticus 16:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Leviticus 16:1-25|25}}). Because of Jesus and his unique role as high priest, he has already entered God’s presence for us. He serves as our eternal high priest and leads us to enter God’s presence with him ({{Hebrews 10:19-23|Hebrews 10:19}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 10:19-23|23}}). 

- *the order of Melchizedek*: This phrase introduces the discussion in {{Hebrews 7:1-28|7:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:1-28|28}}.

- *king of Salem*: See {{Genesis 14:18|Genesis 14:18}} and the related study note. 

- *and priest of God Most High*: Melchizedek was both a king and a priest, unlike the Hebrew kings. This role foreshadowed the Messiah. 

- *returning from the slaughter of the kings*: See {{Genesis 14:1-17|Genesis 14:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Genesis 14:1-17|17}}.
This section proclaims the superiority of Melchizedek’s priesthood over that of the Levites, based primarily on {{Genesis 14:17-20|Genesis 14:17}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Genesis 14:17-20|20}}.

The author of Hebrews talked about Melchizedek and Levi to describe Jesus’ work as a priest.

God established the Jewish priestly system in the Law of Moses. Men from the tribe of Levi served as priests. Men from the family line of Aaron served as high priest. When a high priest died, another man from Aaron’s family line took his place.

Yet verse 4 of Psalm 110 announced that the Messiah would be a priest for ever just like Melchizedek. Melchizedek wasn’t part of the Jewish priestly system. He wasn’t from Levi’s tribe. Melchizedek’s family line isn’t recorded in the Old Testament. For the author of Hebrews, this meant that Melchizedek had no beginning and no end. In this way it’s understood that his service as a priest lasts for ever.

Jesus wasn’t from the tribe of Levi either. As God’s Son, Jesus has no beginning and no end. His service as a priest also lasts for ever. Jesus didn’t become a priest because the Jewish priestly system allowed him to. He became a priest because God promised he would be. He became a priest because he has powerful eternal life that death can’t destroy.

In this way he completes the Jewish priestly system. No one else needs to serve as a priest between God and people. No more sin offerings need to be made for people to be forgiven. Jesus’ sacrifice saves people from the power of sin for ever.
{{Hebrews 7:1-28|Hebrews 7}} expands on the idea from {{Hebrews 5:1-10|5:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 5:1-10|10}}: Jesus is chosen as a high priest like Melchizedek.

- Abraham gave a tenth to the Lord by giving it to Melchizedek, his priest. This act foreshadows the giving of tithes under the law ({{Leviticus 27:30|Leviticus 27:30}}, {{Leviticus 27:32|32}}) and is important in the author's argument ({{Hebrews 7:4|Hebrews 7:4}}). 

- Melchi- (Hebrew *melek*) means king. 

- -zedek (Hebrew *tsedeq*) means justice or righteousness. 

- Salem (Hebrew *shalom*) means peace. Rabbis often highlighted the theological meaning of a biblical figure's name by linking it to other Hebrew terms.

- We have no record of Melchizedek’s family, which is important because the Levitical priesthood required ancestry. He seems to appear from nowhere, as if his life has no beginning or end. The author interprets {{Genesis 14:17-20|Genesis 14:17}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Genesis 14:17-20|20}} with {{Psalm 110:4|Psalm 110:4}}, seeing Melchizedek as symbolizing an eternal priesthood. 

- He remains a priest forever, unlike a Levite whose priesthood ends at death ({{Hebrews 7:8|Hebrews 7:8}}, {{Hebrews 7:23|23}}). 

- *like the Son of God*: Melchizedek was not an Old Testament appearance of Jesus. Instead, his priesthood and the priesthood of Jesus share similar traits, as noted in {{Psalm 110:4|Psalm 110:4}}.

This section ({{Hebrews 7:1-10|Hebrews 7:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:1-10|10}}) asks us to think about how important Melchizedek was by comparing him to Levi's descendants. Melchizedek was so significant that Abraham gave him a tenth of the battle spoils ({{Genesis 14:20|Genesis 14:20}}).

- Collecting the tithe was both a duty and an honor for the priests under the law of Moses ({{Numbers 18:21-32|Numbers 18:21}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Numbers 18:21-32|32}}). 

- *from the people*: This refers to all the people of Israel. 

- Although Melchizedek was not a descendant of Levi, he collected a tenth from Abraham, the ancestor of the Levites. This shows Melchizedek’s greater status over both Abraham and his descendants, including the priests ({{Hebrews 7:8-10|Hebrews 7:8}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:8-10|10}}).

Melchizedek blessed Abraham ({{Genesis 14:19-20|Genesis 14:19}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Genesis 14:19-20|20}}). This blessing is like one a superior gives to a subordinate, such as a father blessing his son or a priest blessing his people ({{Genesis 49:1-28|Genesis 49:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Genesis 49:1-28|28}}; {{Numbers 6:22-27|Numbers 6:22}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Numbers 6:22-27|27}}). The ability to give a blessing shows that Melchizedek is greater than Abraham.
One reason Melchizedek is greater than the Levites is his “immortality” ({{Hebrews 7:3|7:3}}). The Levites were men who died, but Scripture says Melchizedek continues to live.

*And so to speak*: The author knows that saying the Levites paid a tithe to Melchizedek is not literally true, since Levi was not born yet. Abraham represented all his descendants when he paid his tithe to Melchizedek. Levi was connected to Abraham because he came from Abraham's lineage. All of Abraham's descendants were united with him. So, his action could be seen as their action.

In the Letter to the Hebrews, perfection means *achieving a desired goal* rather than being *flawless* (see study note on 5:9). The priesthood under the old covenant could not fulfill all of God's intentions for a covenant relationship with his people. This is why God needed to create a different priesthood.

After explaining why Melchizedek is greater than the Levites ({{Hebrews 7:1-10|Hebrews 7:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:1-10|10}}), the author now argues that Jesus, our high priest like Melchizedek, is also greater than the Levitical priests of the old covenant.

According to the law given to Moses, the appointed priests were descendants of Aaron ({{Exodus 28:41-43|Exodus 28:41}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 28:41-43|43}}; {{Exodus 29:9|29:9}}). The priesthood changed because Jesus is now the high priest. So, God changed the law about priests.
*belonged to a different tribe*: Under the old covenant, priests came from the tribe of Levi, but Jesus was from the tribe of Judah.

This change in how God appoints priests ({{Hebrews 7:11-14|Hebrews 7:11}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:11-14|14}}) is clear through Jesus being appointed as a different kind of priest. Like Melchizedek, Jesus is a priest forever. His resurrection from the dead shows he has the power of an indestructible life. Since his priesthood, in the order of Melchizedek, is superior to the Levites' ({{Hebrews 7:1-10|7:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:1-10|10}}), he replaces them as priest.

- The previous rule for becoming a priest was being part of Aaron's family (see {{Exodus 28:41-43|Exodus 28:41}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 28:41-43|43}}). 

- *set aside*: See {{Hebrews 7:15-17|Hebrews 7:15}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:15-17|17}}. 

- *because it was weak and useless*: This is explained in the following verses ({{Hebrews 7:19-28|7:19}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:19-28|28}}).

*the law made nothing perfect*: The law could not completely remove sin or guarantee eternal salvation. God achieved these things through the superior high priesthood of Jesus.

Because of this, believers have confidence in a better hope and a restored relationship with God. They can draw near to God without fear of condemnation.

The priests under the old covenant were weak because they died, which ended their service, and they were also sinful. In contrast, Jesus is the new high priest. He never sinned and he defeated death, so his priesthood is permanent and more effective.

- This new system is about how God chooses a priest. 

- God’s serious promise is shown in the quote from {{Psalm 110:4|Psalm 110:4}}.

In legal terms, a *guarantee* means taking responsibility for another person’s debt or obligation. The guarantor accepts the risk if the other person fails.

Because God confirmed this promise with an oath, Jesus has a priesthood that cannot be challenged or undone. As a result, our covenant relationship with God is secure. Having Jesus as the guarantee makes the new covenant better.

The old covenant needed many priests because each one eventually died. In contrast, the priesthood of Jesus is* permanent*. This term refers to something unchangeable, like the sun's daily path across the sky or the regular change of seasons.

- *able to save completely*: Since Jesus lives forever, the salvation he offers also lasts forever. To approach an eternal God, we need an eternal priest. 

- Jesus will *intercede* or appeal to God for us as our high priest of the new covenant, and his intercession never ends (see {{Hebrews 9:11-28|Hebrews 9:11}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:11-28|28}}; {{Hebrews 10:21-22|10:21}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 10:21-22|22}}; {{Romans 8:31-34|Romans 8:31}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Romans 8:31-34|34}}).

- Jesus is free from sin and different from sinners (see {{Hebrews 4:15|Hebrews 4:15}}). This makes him better than the old covenant priests, who had to handle their own sins and those of the people (see also {{Hebrews 5:1-3|5:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 5:1-3|3}}). 

- He holds the highest place of honor in heaven, affirming his unique role as high priest (see {{Hebrews 2:9|2:9}}; {{Hebrews 5:9|5:9}}; {{Philippians 2:5-11|Philippians 2:5}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Philippians 2:5-11|11}}). 

- *once for all*: This means *once, never to be repeated*, not *once for all people*.

- This verse summarizes the discussion in {{Hebrews 5:1-3|5:1–3}}about Christ's role as High Priest ({{Hebrews 5:1-10|5:1–10}}; {{Hebrews 7:1-28|7:1–28}}). 

- Limited by human weakness refers primarily to human sinfulness and mortality. 

- God appointed his Son, Jesus, with an oath (see {{Psalm 110:4|Psalm 110:4}}, which is important for understanding {{Hebrews 7:11-28|Hebrews 7:11–28}}).

- In Hebrews, the term perfect means *complete* or *mature* (see {{Hebrews 2:10|2:10}}; {{Hebrews 5:9|5:9}}; {{Hebrews 7:11|7:11}}; {{Hebrews 9:9-11|9:9–11}}); the Son, through his sacrificial death and resurrection, has become completely qualified to serve as our eternal High Priest, and his priesthood lasts forever.

- The first two verses of chapter {{Hebrews 8:1-13|8}} connect the previous discussion and introduce the next topic. 

- The main point is that Jesus is appointed as a superior high priest ({{Hebrews 5:1-10|Hebrews 5:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 5:1-10|10}}; {{Hebrews 7:1-28|7:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:1-28|28}}). 

- He serves in the heavenly tabernacle (also in {{Hebrews 8:5|8:5}}): This introduces the theme of Jesus’s superior offering, discussed in the rest of this section ({{Hebrews 8:3-10:18|8:3–10:18}}). Unlike the Levitical priests who served in an earthly tent or building, the sacrifice of Jesus is superior because he serves in the true place of worship, the very presence of God in heaven ({{Hebrews 8:5|8:5}}; {{Hebrews 9:11|9:11}}, {{Hebrews 9:24|24}}; {{Hebrews 10:12|10:12}}).

God established the Mount Sinai covenant with the people of Israel through Moses. The author of Hebrews called it both the old covenant and the first covenant. It was based on laws that the Israelites had to obey. The Jewish priestly system was part of that covenant.

Before the temple was built, Israelite priests served in the holy tent. The tent and the temple were based on what is in heaven. They were built as a copy of the holy place where God rules as King. That is where Jesus does his work as a high priest. He serves as the high priest and go-between of God’s new covenant with his people.

The new covenant doesn’t depend on people obeying God’s laws. It depends on God changing people from inside their heart. The Mount Sinai covenant is finished now that God has made the new covenant.
This passage explains that the role of Jesus as the heavenly high priest is better than the role of earthly priests.

- Every high priest must offer gifts and sacrifices. Since offering sacrifices is a general duty of priests, Jesus also needed to offer a sacrifice. 

- This verse repeats what was mentioned in the first verse of the earlier discussion ({{Hebrews 5:1|Hebrews 5:1}}), marking another important section in the book.

If Jesus were on earth, he would not be a priest under the old system (see {{Hebrews 7:13-14|Hebrews 7:13}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:13-14|14}}). However, Jesus is in heaven, making his priestly role unique and better than the priests of the old covenant ({{Hebrews 8:5|8:5}}; {{Hebrews 9:11|9:11}}, {{Hebrews 9:24|24}}; {{Hebrews 10:12|10:12}}).

*a copy and shadow*: The earthly place of worship was a copy of the real one in heaven. This is why God told Moses to follow the pattern (see {{Exodus 25:40|Exodus 25:40}}; {{Exodus 26:30|26:30}}; compare {{Acts 7:44|Acts 7:44}}). Both Judaism and early Christianity talked about a heavenly temple in a heavenly Jerusalem, which would come to earth at the end of time (see {{Revelation 21:2|Revelation 21:2}}). Hebrews suggests that God showed Moses this heavenly place so he could build the earthly tabernacle. However, Jesus serves as high priest in the heavenly temple.

- *He mediates*: A mediator helps two parties reach an agreement. Christ's sacrifice created a covenant (agreement) between people and God. 

- *the covenant He mediates is better*: See “The New Covenant” Theme Note. This covenant is better because it relies on better promises (see {{Hebrews 8:7-13|Hebrews 8:7}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 8:7-13|13}}).

The first agreement, made at Mount Sinai, was not without faults. It was only part of God’s plan, because it did not overcome human weakness (see {{Hebrews 7:11-28|Hebrews 7:11}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:11-28|28}}; {{Hebrews 8:9|8:9}}).

The author refers to {{Jeremiah 31:31-34|Jeremiah 31:31}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Jeremiah 31:31-34|34}}, an Old Testament prophecy about the new covenant with several important promises. Highlighting the new covenant's superiority supports the argument in {{Hebrews 9:1-10:18|Hebrews 9:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:1-10:18|10:18}} that the Son’s offering under the new covenant was better than the old covenant offerings.
*God found fault with the people*: The people could not follow the old agreement's terms (see study note on Hebrews 8:7), so God created a new agreement.

- God made a covenant with their ancestors at Sinai ({{Exodus 19:1-8|Exodus 19:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 19:1-8|8}}; {{Exodus 24:7-8|24:7}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 24:7-8|8}}; {{Exodus 34:27-28|34:27}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 34:27-28|28}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:13|Deuteronomy 4:13}}). 

- *I took them by the hand*: God rescued his people from Egypt, guiding them like a parent guides a child who cannot care for itself (see {{Exodus 12:1-14:31|Exodus 12–14}}). 

- *they did not abide by My covenant*: See {{Hebrews 3:7-19|Hebrews 3:7}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 3:7-19|19}}; {{Numbers 14:1-38|Numbers 14:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Numbers 14:1-38|38}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:1-29|Deuteronomy 9}}; {{Psalm 106:1-48|Psalms 106}}.

- *I disregarded them*: The covenant warned that if the people turned away, God would also turn away from them (see {{Deuteronomy 28:15-68|Deuteronomy 28:15}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Deuteronomy 28:15-68|68}}; {{Deuteronomy 30:11-20|30:11}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Deuteronomy 30:11-20|20}}; {{1 Kings 8:22-53|1 Kings 8:22}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{1 Kings 8:22-53|53}}; {{2 Chronicles 6:12-42|2 Chronicles 6:12}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{2 Chronicles 6:12-42|42}}).

In the old covenant, people had to deeply understand the words of the law ({{Deuteronomy 32:46|Deuteronomy 32:46}}). The kings of Israel and Judah were judged on their dedication to God's law ({{2 Kings 10:31|2 Kings 10:31}}; {{2 Chronicles 31:21|2 Chronicles 31:21}}). Under the new covenant, God's laws are meant to be in people's minds and hearts. People would have renewed hearts and minds, with God's law as a natural, internal motivation.
All people in the new covenant know the Lord. A close and personal relationship with him is at the center of the new covenant.

A key feature of the new covenant is that God will forgive their wickedness and never again remember their sins. The sacrifice of Jesus fully cleanses his people from sin ({{Hebrews 9:13-15|Hebrews 9:13}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:13-15|15}}; {{Hebrews 10:14-18|10:14}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 10:14-18|18}}, {{Hebrews 10:22|22}}; {{1 John 1:7|1 John 1:7}}).
The word *new* in "new" covenant emphasizes that, after God established this covenant, the Sinai covenant became old or *obselete*. Its usefulness ended, and it was about to be replaced.
These verses describe the tabernacle, which was Israel's place of worship before they built the temple.

The Mount Sinai covenant was like a will that went into effect at death. The death wasn’t the death of people but of animals that God provided. This showed that God loved people and didn’t want them to die because of their sins.

The Mount Sinai covenant wasn’t supposed to last for ever. It was a sign of greater things that would come. It pointed to the Messiah and to his work. The new covenant also went into effect at death. The death wasn’t the death of people or animals but of Jesus Christ. Jesus sacrificed himself to establish the new covenant. This shows how deeply God loves people.

In the Mount Sinai covenant, people were sprinkled with animal blood. This allowed them to be considered clean. It made them able to enter the holy tent. In the new covenant, people are sprinkled with Jesus’ blood. Believers don’t actually feel Jesus’ real blood on them. This is a way of describing what happens spiritually when Jesus saves people.

Jesus’ blood is much more powerful than the blood of animals. His blood makes those who believe in him completely clean and accepted for ever. Jesus forgives them. He heals what sin and evil have done to their mind and heart. The author of Hebrews described this as washing away feelings of guilt. Jesus makes people able to be with God fully and for ever. That is how Jesus will make their salvation complete when he returns.

This section explains that Christ's death, as the sacrifice in the new covenant, is better than the sacrifices in the old covenant. In {{Hebrews 9:1-10|Hebrews 9:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:1-10|10}}, the author describes worship practices under the old covenant rules (see {{Exodus 28:1-29:46|Exodus 28}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 28:1-29:46|29}}; {{Leviticus 1:1-10:20|Leviticus 1–10}}; {{Leviticus 16:1-17:16|16:1–17:16}}). In {{Hebrews 9:11-10:18|Hebrews 9:11–10:18}}, these rules are compared to Christ's superior offering.

- Israel's tabernacle was a tent with two rooms (see {{Exodus 25:1-31:18|Exodus 25}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 25:1-31:18|31}}; {{Exodus 35:1-40:38|35:1–40:38}}). 

- *the lampstand*: {{Exodus 25:31-40|Exodus 25:31}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 25:31-40|40}}; {{Exodus 26:35|26:35}}. 

- *the table*: {{Exodus 25:23-30|Exodus 25:23}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 25:23-30|30}}. 

- The priests entered the Holy Place daily to perform their ritual duties ({{Hebrews 9:6|Hebrews 9:6}}; see {{Exodus 28:43|Exodus 28:43}}; {{Numbers 28:3-8|Numbers 28:3}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Numbers 28:3-8|8}}).

At the back of the first room of the tabernacle was a curtain that separated it from the second room, called the Most Holy Place ({{Exodus 26:31-33|Exodus 26:31}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 26:31-33|33}}). This curtain was a sacred barrier. Only the high priest could go behind it into the Most Holy Place, and only once a year on the Day of Atonement ({{Hebrews 9:7|Hebrews 9:7}}; see {{Exodus 30:6|Exodus 30:6}}, {{Exodus 30:10|10}}; {{Leviticus 16:2-34|Leviticus 16:2–34}}; {{Leviticus 23:27-32|23:27}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Leviticus 23:27-32|32}}).

- The gold incense altar likely stood just outside the inner curtain ({{Exodus 30:1-10|Exodus 30:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 30:1-10|10}}). Its exact location is unclear in the Old Testament, but it was closely linked to the Most Holy Place ({{Exodus 30:6|Exodus 30:6}}; {{Leviticus 16:13|Leviticus 16:13}}; {{1 Kings 6:22|1 Kings 6:22}}). 

- The ark of the covenant, representing God's presence, was the most important item in the tabernacle (see {{Exodus 25:10-22|Exodus 25:10}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 25:10-22|22}}). 

- The gold jar with manna reminded people of God's provision in the wilderness ({{Exodus 16:32-34|Exodus 16:32}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 16:32-34|34}}). 

- Aaron’s staff, which sprouted leaves (see {{Numbers 17:1-11|Numbers 17:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Numbers 17:1-11|11}}), reminded people not to rebel against God's chosen leaders ({{Numbers 17:10|Numbers 17:10}}; compare {{Hebrews 13:17|Hebrews 13:17}}). 

- The stone tablets of the covenant held the Ten Commandments and reminded the people of the rules they were to live by ({{Exodus 25:16|Exodus 25:16}}; {{Exodus 31:18|31:18}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:9-10:5|Deuteronomy 9:9–10:5}}).

- The cherubim of divine glory were angel statues on the cover of the ark. These angels are closely linked to God's glorious presence ({{Genesis 3:24|Genesis 3:24}}; {{Psalm 80:1|Psalms 80:1}}; {{Psalm 99:1|99:1}}; {{Isaiah 37:16|Isaiah 37:16}}). The ark's cover was the atonement place, where they sprinkled blood from the Day of Atonement sacrifice ({{Leviticus 16:14-16|Leviticus 16:14–16}}). 

- *we cannot discuss these things in detail now*: The main topic is the offering of sacrifices under the old covenant ({{Hebrews 9:6-10|Hebrews 9:6}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:6-10|10}}).

In the Holy Place, which was the first room of the tabernacle ({{Hebrews 9:2|Hebrews 9:2}}), priests had specific duties. They kept the lamps burning and replaced the sacred loaves of bread regularly ({{Exodus 27:20-21|Exodus 27:20}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 27:20-21|21}}; {{Leviticus 24:8|Leviticus 24:8}}).

Each year on the Day of Atonement, the high priest offered sacrifices for sins not covered by other sacrifices from the past year ({{Leviticus 16:1-25|Leviticus 16:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Leviticus 16:1-25|25}}).

- *had not yet been disclosed*: Under the old covenant system, people could not freely enter God's presence. 

- The outer room of the tabernacle, which served as a sacred barrier, kept people from entering the Most Holy Place. This barrier symbolized the entire system, which kept people away from God's presence instead of guiding them into it.

This example shows that the gifts and sacrifices of the old covenant could not clear people's consciences. They could not remove guilt before a holy God (see {{Hebrews 9:14|9:14}}; {{Hebrews 10:2|10:2}}, {{Hebrews 10:22|22}}; {{Hebrews 13:18|13:18}}).

The old system focused only on physical rules and could not address people's inner feelings ({{Hebrews 8:10|Hebrews 8:10}}; {{Hebrews 10:21-24|10:21}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 10:21-24|24}}). It was temporary, meant to last until Christ came to create a better system ({{Hebrews 9:11-10:18|9:11–10:18}}).

- Christ is now the high priest over all the good things of the new covenant. God appointed him, as mentioned in {{Psalm 110:4|Psalm 110:4}} ({{Hebrews 5:1-10|Hebrews 5:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 5:1-10|10}}; {{Hebrews 7:1-28|7:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 7:1-28|28}}), and he offered a better sacrifice. 

- *that have come*: Some manuscripts say *that are about to come,* either from the old covenant's viewpoint or looking forward to God's future plan. 

- Christ’s sacrifice is better because it was made in the greater, perfect tabernacle in heaven, not the earthly one (see {{Hebrews 8:5|8:5}} and corresponding study note).

The author compares the old system ({{Hebrews 9:1-10|Hebrews 9:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:1-10|10}}) with Christ's superior sacrifice as high priest. Christ offered his own blood, not animal blood ({{Hebrews 9:13-22|9:13}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:13-22|22}}; see also {{Hebrews 9:7|9:7}}). His offering took place in the heavenly tabernacle, not the earthly one ({{Hebrews 9:23-24|9:23}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:23-24|24}}; see also {{Hebrews 9:1-5|9:1}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:1-5|5}}). Unlike repeated offerings, Christ's sacrifice happened only once ({{Hebrews 9:25-10:18|9:25–10:18}}; see also {{Hebrews 7:27|7:27}}; {{Hebrews 9:6-7|9:6}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:6-7|7}}).

- Christ's offering is better because he used his own blood, not the blood of goats and calves (see {{Leviticus 16:3-5|Leviticus 16:3}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Leviticus 16:3-5|5}}). 

- Christ's offering is better because he entered the Most Holy Place once for all time. Unlike the sacrifices in the old covenant, which had to be repeated every year ({{Hebrews 10:1|Hebrews 10:1}}), the sacrificial death of Jesus was needed only once and secured our redemption forever.
The ashes of a young cow were mixed with water to purify people from ceremonial impurity (see {{Numbers 19:1-22|Numbers 19}}).

- *how much more*: This is an argument from lesser to greater, a traditional Jewish way of reasoning. The idea is that if something is true in a smaller case, it is even more true in a bigger case (see also {{Hebrews 2:1-4|Hebrews 2:1–4}}; {{Hebrews 12:25-29|12:25}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 12:25-29|29}}). If animal blood had some effect in cleansing, then Christ's blood will be much more effective. 

- *purify our consciences*: Christ’s sacrifice, unlike the old covenant sacrifices, removes the guilt that keeps us from God by thoroughly cleansing us from sinful actions.

*the mediator*: This term describes a person who helps resolve a tough legal or political disagreement. In the old covenant, people saw Moses and the angels as go-betweens between God and the people ({{Galatians 3:19-20|Galatians 3:19}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Galatians 3:19-20|20}}). In the new covenant, Christ connects God and people through his sacrificial death ({{Hebrews 8:6|Hebrews 8:6}}; {{Hebrews 12:24|12:24}}; {{Romans 6:23|Romans 6:23}}; {{1 Timothy 2:5|1 Timothy 2:5}}; {{1 Peter 3:18|1 Peter 3:18}}) and ongoing intercession (prayer on behalf of others) ({{Hebrews 7:25|Hebrews 7:25}}).

The author explains a basic rule about wills or covenants ({{Hebrews 9:16-17|Hebrews 9:16}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:16-17|17}}). He then discusses it further, using the start of the first covenant as an example ({{Hebrews 9:18-22|9:18}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:18-22|22}}).

- *put into effect*: {{Exodus 24:3-8|Exodus 24:3}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 24:3-8|8}} describes Moses starting the old covenant using the blood of a sacrifice. 

- Hebrews is the only ancient source that says Moses sprinkled the book of God's law (see {{Exodus 24:6-8|Exodus 24:6}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Exodus 24:6-8|8}}). 

- Hyssop branches have blue flowers and strong-smelling leaves. People used them with sacrifices for cleansing ({{Exodus 12:22|Exodus 12:22}}; {{Leviticus 14:4|Leviticus 14:4}}; {{Numbers 19:6|Numbers 19:6}}, {{Numbers 19:18|18}}).

“This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you” ({{Exodus 24:8|Exodus 24:8}}): Jesus used similar words at the Last Supper, talking about his own death ({{Matthew 26:28|Matthew 26:28}}; {{Mark 14:24|Mark 14:24}}; {{1 Corinthians 11:25|1 Corinthians 11:25}}).

In the law of Moses, many cleansing rituals required the death of a sacrificial animal. Blood was used in these cleansing rituals (see {{Exodus 29:12|Exodus 29:12}}; {{Exodus 30:10|30:10}}; {{Leviticus 4:6|Leviticus 4:6}}, {{Leviticus 4:17|17}}; {{Leviticus 16:14-19|16:14}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Leviticus 16:14-19|19}}; {{Numbers 19:4|Numbers 19:4}}) and for making atonement (see {{Leviticus 16:1-34|Leviticus 16}}). The shedding of Christ’s blood created the new covenant, offering lasting purification and complete forgiveness of sins ({{Hebrews 8:12|Hebrews 8:12}}; {{Hebrews 10:15-18|10:15–18}}; {{Matthew 26:28|Matthew 26:28}}; {{Ephesians 1:7|Ephesians 1:7}}).

- This verse uses a comparison from lesser to greater (see study note on Hebrews 9:14). Just as heaven is greater than the earthly tabernacle, Christ’s sacrifice had to be much better than earthly sacrifices. 

- *So it was necessary*: See {{Hebrews 9:16-22|9:16}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Hebrews 9:16-22|22}}; {{Leviticus 16:14-19|Leviticus 16:14}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Leviticus 16:14-19|19}}. 

- *copies of the heavenly things*: See study note on Hebrews 8:5. 

- *heavenly things to be purified*: Just as the tabernacle needed cleansing because of the Israelites' sin ({{Leviticus 16:16-19|Leviticus 16:16}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{Leviticus 16:16-19|19}}), the heavenly tabernacle required removing uncleanness from those entering heaven under the new covenant.

Under the new covenant, Christ did not offer his sacrifice in the earthly tabernacle. Instead, he entered God's presence in heaven to act for us. His sacrifice makes him a better mediator to help us have a right relationship with God ({{2 Corinthians 5:19-21|2 Corinthians 5:19}}{{Hebrews 7:20-22|–}}{{2 Corinthians 5:19-21|21}}).
